subject: CuraHealth private GPU pool — performance commitments & networking caveats

Subject: CuraHealth private GPU pool — performance commitments & networking caveats

Hi Sofia,

Thanks for the productive call earlier. As requested, I wanted to outline the specific throughput targets we can commit to for a CuraHealth private deployment and call out the networking constraints that will materially affect peak-percentile latency and sustained throughput. I attached a simple matrix (cura_network_matrix_v1.xlsx) with the scenarios and a short draft of the commitment language (throughput_commitment_draft.pdf).

Summary of what we believe is achievable for a dedicated private GPU pool in your VPC (baseline assumptions: 8x A100-equivalent GPUs per pool, single-tenant shard, optimistic kernel choices):
- Sustained throughput target (99th token latency < 250ms): 1200 tokens/sec aggregate per pool for batched, mixed-size requests (avg seq length 128).
- Peak absorb (short spikes up to 30s): up to 2400 tokens/sec with warm cache + burst lanes, subject to network egress and NIC oversubscription constraints.
- Warmup behavior: cold start for larger KV caches will see degraded throughput for ~20–90s depending on model size; we recommend prefix warming for any predictable steady-state windows.

Critical network caveats (please review with your infra/procurement):
1) Egress shaping: if your VPC outbound is NAT-gated with burst policers, observed tail latencies can increase by 3–6x for spike windows. We need the ability to reserve a burst lane or a higher egress bucket for the pool.
2) Cross-AZ traffic: if the GPU hosts are spread across AZs, we recommend cross-AZ placement only for DR — production throughput should prefer single-AZ placement to avoid added jitter.
3) NIC oversubscription: some cloud flavors report high NIC oversubscription at 75% utilization; we’ll need explicit confirmation of NIC ratios or a plan to pin nodes with dedicated NICs.

Next steps I propose:
- Cura team to confirm egress bucket and NAT policy (who to loop in?).
- We’ll run a 2-hour soak test with your staging VPC to validate the burst curves.
- If you’re comfortable with the numbers, we’ll fold the throughput rows into the SOW and attach the warmup/operational notes as an appendix.

I’m copying Rishi and Karthik for the operational details and to flag anything I missed.

Best,
Laura
Laura Bennett
Head, Product Operations — Redwood Inference
laura_bennett@redwood.com

Laura —

Really helpful summary, thank you. A few clarifying points from our side after an infra sync this morning:
- Procurement will need the 'peak absorb' definition written into the SOW with clear runbook triggers (we can accept a 30s window but need explicit failover behavior documented).
- Our VPC NAT is currently on a shared gateway with burst policing (60 MB/s sustained, 200 MB/s burst) — I’ll get exact docs from our networking team. We may be able to carve a private egress IP pool if Redwood requires it.
- Cross-AZ: we prefer single-AZ for production but want DR across a second AZ; your suggestion aligns.
- Cold cache warmup: can Redwood provide a warmup API call pattern we can integrate into our deployment CI so we pre-warm before scheduled batch windows?

Also, question on measurements: is the 'tokens/sec' metric measured at the Redwood API ingress (post- batching) or at the model host (token emission)? We need consistent contract language for SLA calculations.

Ben from procurement will coordinate the SOW language and I'll follow up with the networking artifact.

Thanks,
Sofia Ramos
Director, Applied ML — CuraHealth
sofia.ramos@curahealth.com

Rishi/Karthik — quick proposals:
1) SLA metric: define 'aggregate tokens/sec measured at Redwood ingress (post-batching) per-pool'. That avoids host-side measurement differences and aligns to customer-perceived throughput. We add a clause that excludes degraded performance due to customer-side egress policing or cross-AZ network incidents.
2) Peak absorb: make it explicit as a 'best-effort commitment' for 30s windows and instrument an automated fallback to a smaller model variant after 35s if buffer drains.
3) Warmup API: we can offer a simple '/v1/admin/pools/{id}/warmup' endpoint that walks through prefix cache seeding and KV prefetch; include a 1k-token synthetic run for each active model. Docs and example curl snippet to ship with SOW.
4) Testing: we should propose a 2-hour staging soak with telemetry (per-route latency percentiles, NIC metrics, egress counters). Add a brief test-plan appendix.

I want to keep the SOW language conservative (avoid hard promises on anything influenced by Cura networking config). Can you draft the short SLA paragraph + the warmup API spec text by EOD Monday? I can then work with Ben on inserting it into procurement redlines.

Laura

From: rishi_malhotra@redwood.com
To: laura_bennett@redwood.com, karthik_iyer@redwood.com, Sofia Ramos <sofia.ramos@curahealth.com>, Ben Porter <ben.porter@curahealth.com>

Subject: Re: CuraHealth private GPU pool — performance commitments & networking caveats

Thanks Laura — I wrote the SLA text and warmup API blurb and attached a minimal test-plan (see drive link). High-level points I added to the SOW draft:
- Measurement: "Throughput" = aggregated tokens emitted per second, measured at Redwood ingress after batching; latency SLOs defined at p50/p95/p99 with carve-outs for customer-side egress or cross-AZ network events.
- Failure modes: explicit exclusion for prolonged NAT egress policing and for cloud NIC oversubscription events outside Redwood's control.
- Peak absorb: stated as a "best-effort buffer" (30s) with automated model-shift fallback and circuit-breaker thresholds documented.
- Warmup API: example curl posted, recommended sequence: model list -> 1k token synthetic warm -> prefix seeding -> KV prefetch.

Link to draft: https://drive.redwoodinternal.com/file/d/1A2B3C-curanet-network-matrix

Sofia/Ben — if that aligns, Laura and I can move this into the procurement doc and include the soak test as an acceptance activity.

-rishi
